```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    fig.align = "center",
    out.width = "100%",
    fig.width = 11,
    fig.height = 7,
    warning = FALSE,
    message = FALSE
)
```

`MicroBioMeta` computes diversity and returns the figure ready for publication. This tutorial explains the Hill-number framework and how to use it in the functions that work with it: `alpha_hill_plot()` and `alpha_diversity_plot()` for alpha diversity, and `beta_ord_plot()` and `beta_test_table()` for beta diversity. The calculations with a tree or with traits come from `hilldiv3` [@alberdi2019guide].

## Why Hill numbers

Hill numbers [@hill1973diversity; @jost2007partitioning] express diversity as an **effective number**: how many equally abundant taxa would give the same diversity as the sample. A sample with a value of 10 is twice as diverse as one with a value of 5, a statement that does not hold for the Shannon or Simpson indices.

The order $q$ sets how much weight the abundances get:

| Order | Weight of the taxa | Equivalent to |
|---|---|---|
| $q = 0$ | All count the same | Richness |
| $q = 1$ | In proportion to their abundance | Exponential of Shannon |
| $q = 2$ | Mostly the dominant ones | Inverse of Simpson |

The same idea extends to two other dimensions of diversity. Here each one has its own unit, so **the values of the three types cannot be compared with each other**: compare groups within a type.

| `diversity` | What it takes into account | What you need | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"taxonomic"` | Abundances | The table | Effective number of features |
| `"phylogenetic"` | How related the taxa are [@chao2010phylogenetic] | Rooted tree | Effective number of lineages |
| `"functional"` | How different their traits are [@chao2019attribute] | Traits per taxon | Effective number of functionally distinct features |

## Preparing the data

We use the fungal example of the package (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, 18S).

```{r data}
library(MicroBioMeta)

table_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "table_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
)
taxonomy_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "taxonomy_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    check.names = FALSE
)
metadata_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "metadata_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    check.names = FALSE
)
metadata_fungi <- metadata_fungi[metadata_fungi$SAMPLEID %in% colnames(table_fungi), ]
table_fungi <- table_fungi[, metadata_fungi$SAMPLEID]

table_fung <- merge_feature_taxonomy(table = table_fungi, taxonomy = taxonomy_fungi)
```

### The tree

The tip labels must be the taxa of the table. With QIIME 2 [@bolyen2019qiime2], the tree comes from the representative sequences, and `exported-tree/tree.nwk` is what you read in R:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
qiime phylogeny align-to-tree-mafft-fasttree \
    --i-sequences rep-seqs.qza \
    --output-dir phylogeny
qiime tools export --input-path phylogeny/rooted_tree.qza --output-path exported-tree
```

```{r tree}
tree_fungi <- ape::read.tree(
    system.file("extdata", "tree_fungi.nwk", package = "MicroBioMeta")
)
```

Check the tree before you use it: a few spurious sequences on a very long branch can flatten $q = 1$ and $q = 2$, because that branch dominates the tree. In this example we removed three *Unassigned* ASVs (10 reads) for that reason.

### The traits

`traits` is a table with taxa in rows and traits in columns. Any measured trait works. For microbial communities a common source is the table of gene families predicted per ASV by PICRUSt2 [@douglas2020picrust2], such as `EC_predicted.tsv`. Those are predictions, not measurements, so report them as such.

```{r traits}
traits_fungi <- read.delim(
    system.file("extdata", "traits_fungi.txt", package = "MicroBioMeta"),
    row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE
)
```

Taxa that are in the table but not in the tree or the traits are dropped with a warning that says how many. Here that happens with the three ASVs above.

## Alpha diversity with Hill numbers

`alpha_hill_plot()` uses the same call for all three types. Only `diversity` and its input change, and the y-axis title follows the unit of each type.

```{r alpha-tax}
alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE
)
```

```{r alpha-phylo}
alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)
```

```{r alpha-func}
alpha_hill_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    facet_by = "Treatment",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi,
    stat = "kruskal.test"
)
```

Two details of these values:

- The phylogenetic values are read at one common tree depth, so samples are comparable. For that reason a sample can fall slightly below 1.
- Functional values depend on a distance threshold; here it is the largest distance between two taxa, the default of `hilldiv3`.

## Classic indices

`alpha_diversity_plot()` shows the classic indices, also with `diversity`:

| `diversity` | Index | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"taxonomic"` | Chao1, Shannon, Simpson | Richness and evenness | Different in each index |
| `"phylogenetic"` | Faith's PD [@faith1992conservation] | Summed branch length up to the root | Branch length |
| `"functional"` | Rao's Q [@rao1982diversity] | Mean distance between two random reads | Distance (Gower) |

```{r classic-phylo, fig.height=4}
alpha_diversity_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)
```

```{r classic-func, fig.height=4}
alpha_diversity_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    x_col = "Type_of_soil",
    fill_col = "Type_of_soil",
    show_legend = FALSE,
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi
)
```

These indices are related to the Hill numbers but they are not the same quantity. Faith's PD is the phylogenetic $q = 0$ before dividing by the depth of the tree, and Rao's Q gives the functional $q = 2$ through $1 / (1 - Q / \tau)$, where $\tau$ is the distance threshold. Choose the classic index if you need to compare with studies that report it, and the Hill number if you want every type in the same framework.

## Beta diversity

### The metrics

`hilldiv3::hillpair()` turns the Hill numbers into dissimilarities between samples [@jost2007partitioning; @chiu2014phylogenetic]. In `MicroBioMeta` they are one more option of `distance`, next to `"jaccard"` or `"aitchison"`, with the order set by `q`. They range from 0 (identical samples) to 1 (nothing shared), so they have no unit problem.

| `distance` | Type | $q = 0$ | $q = 1$ | $q = 2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"U"` | Jaccard type | Jaccard | Horn | Regional overlap |
| `"C"` | Sørensen type | Sørensen | Horn | Morisita-Horn |
| `"V"` | Sørensen-type turnover | Sørensen | | |
| `"S"` | Jaccard-type turnover | Jaccard | | |

With `diversity = "phylogenetic"` and $q = 0$, `"U"` is the unweighted UniFrac [@lozupone2005unifrac]. It is a good default if you already use Jaccard. At $q = 1$ it is related to the weighted UniFrac, but it is not the same value.

These metrics describe the differences in Hill-number terms; they are not compositional. If your main analysis uses CLR/Aitchison, keep it there and use these as a complement.

### Ordination

The Hill metrics work with `ordination = "PCoA"` or `"NMDS"`, the same as any distance that is not `"compositional"`.

```{r ord-tax, fig.height=5}
beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 1,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil"
)
```

```{r ord-phylo, fig.height=5}
beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil",
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)
```

```{r ord-func, fig.height=5}
beta_ord_plot(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    distance = "U",
    q = 1,
    ordination = "PCoA",
    group_col = "Type_of_soil",
    diversity = "functional",
    traits = traits_fungi
)
```

### PERMANOVA and betadisper

`beta_test_table()` takes the same arguments. A PERMANOVA [@anderson2001permanova] tests whether the groups differ, and betadisper [@anderson2006distance] whether their dispersion does. Report both: a significant PERMANOVA with unequal dispersions may reflect differences in dispersion, not in position. In this example betadisper is significant, so read the PERMANOVA of `Type_of_soil` with that in mind.

```{r permanova}
beta_test_table(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    formula_str = "Type_of_soil * Treatment",
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)
```

```{r betadisper}
beta_test_table(
    table = table_fung,
    metadata = metadata_fungi,
    formula_str = "Type_of_soil",
    distance = "U",
    q = 0,
    test = "betadisper",
    diversity = "phylogenetic",
    tree = tree_fungi
)
```
